sources.name: Computational Complexity
sources.title: VP ≠ VNP

stories.headline: Anthropic posts Lean-verified proof that VP does not equal VNP
stories.dek: A blog post at Computational Complexity calls the algebraic permanent-versus-determinant separation the year's most important complexity result, though P vs NP stays open.
stories.body:
Anthropic has released a proof, verified in the Lean proof assistant, that VP does not equal VNP. The Computational Complexity blog calls it, for now, the most important computational complexity result of 2026. Whether VP equals VNP is the algebraic analog of the P versus NP question.

The question comes down to two near-identical formulas. The determinant of a matrix sums products of its entries with alternating signs. It can be computed efficiently, and Berkowitz's algorithm does it with only additions and multiplications, which puts it in VP: polynomials computable by polynomial-size algebraic circuits. The permanent is the same formula without the signs. Leslie Valiant showed computing it is #P-complete, as hard as counting solutions to an NP problem. He also showed it is complete for VNP, the class built from exponential sums of VP polynomials.

According to the blog, Anthropic's paper shows the permanent of an n-by-n matrix needs algebraic circuits of size 2 to the power of Omega((log n)^(4/3)), more than any polynomial. That settles Valiant's original question too: the permanent cannot be written as the determinant of a polynomial-size matrix of variables and constants.

The method is unexpected. The Mulmuley-Sohoni Geometric Complexity Theory program proposed attacking the problem with algebraic geometry and representation theory. Anthropic's proof uses essentially none of that, the blog says. It uses a variant of Strassen's asymptotic spectrum to split the problem into two cases, one handled by a rank argument and the other by diagonalization. The blog's author says he cannot say what this means for the GCT program.

The result does not crack P versus NP. The closest Boolean analog would be that #P functions lack polynomial-size circuits of depth O((log n)^2), and VP not equal to VNP does not imply even that. Algebraic circuits may be much weaker than ordinary ones. Checking whether a simple AND-OR circuit is satisfiable is NP-complete, while checking whether a VP circuit computes a nonzero polynomial takes randomized polynomial time.

The blog calls the result a major step toward complexity lower bounds but says it offers no technique for the full power of computation. Settling P versus NP, it concludes, "remains far out of reach for man or machine."
key_points: Anthropic released a Lean-verified proof that VP does not equal VNP
Permanent needs algebraic circuits of size 2^Ω((log n)^4/3)
Proof skips algebraic geometry, using Strassen's asymptotic spectrum and diagonalization
Result does not imply a Boolean separation or resolve P vs NP
stories.why_it_matters: An AI lab producing a machine-checked proof of a decades-old open problem shows formal verification tools like Lean being used for frontier mathematics. P versus NP, and the cryptography that rests on hardness assumptions, are untouched.

sources.title: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach

stories.headline: 1Password says GitHub account breach exposed customer data and code
stories.dek: An attacker used a hijacked employee GitHub account to push malicious code to backend services, but the company says vaults stayed sealed.
stories.body:
1Password has disclosed a breach in which an attacker took over an employee's corporate GitHub account, pushed malicious code to backend services and downloaded account records for a subset of its customers. The company says no vault contents, account recovery keys or the keys that protect vaults were accessed.

The company began investigating on November 19 and published its disclosure on November 25. It says the stolen records include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and non-secret internal metadata. 1Password says the SRP parameters cannot be used to access an account and that public keys are public by design.

The records also held tokens from emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery. 1Password says these tokens cannot open an account on their own, because completing the process also requires an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to the user's registered email. A small number of users had pending invitations or recoveries during the incident and have been notified individually. As a precaution, the company has lengthened those codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and got into the CI/CD system. 1Password says its source code contains no user secrets, but acknowledges that CI/CD holds infrastructure secrets, and says it has rotated or revoked every credential that may have been exposed. It has disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services and tightened GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls. Independent security experts are validating the cleanup, and the company says it has found no evidence of account takeovers.

Customers do not need to change passwords or Secret Keys, according to 1Password. BleepingComputer warns that the stolen data still amounts to a list of known 1Password users, which is useful for phishing campaigns that use the breach as a lure. The company has not said how many customers fall into the affected subset or how the GitHub account was compromised. BleepingComputer says its questions to 1Password have not yet been answered.
key_points: Hijacked employee GitHub account used to push malicious code to backend
Names, emails, IDs and recovery tokens taken for a subset of users
Private source code copied and CI/CD system accessed
1Password says vaults, keys and recovery keys were not accessed
stories.why_it_matters: The vault encryption design appears to have held, but known 1Password users are now likely phishing targets. Treat any email about invitations or account recovery with suspicion and open the app directly. For developers, the breach is another case of one compromised GitHub account reaching production through CI/CD.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf]

stories.headline: Preprint in OpenAI math repo claims polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false
stories.dek: The paper argues some simple polytopes have superpolynomial graph diameter, a claim that would limit the simplex method but awaits expert checking.
stories.body:
A preprint posted to OpenAI's public math repository on GitHub claims to disprove the polynomial Hirsch conjecture, a long-standing open problem in geometry and optimization. The paper, titled "Superpolynomial graph diameter of simple polytopes" and dated November 24, 2026, sits in the repository's preprints folder. It drew attention on Hacker News under the blunt title "The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false."

The claim has not been independently verified. A preprint is not peer reviewed, and results of this size usually take specialists weeks or months to check. The repository does not say who wrote the paper, how it was produced or what role, if any, AI models played.

The conjecture concerns polytopes, the multidimensional shapes formed by a set of linear inequalities. Their corners and edges form a graph, and the diameter of that graph is the largest number of edge steps needed to travel between any two corners. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture holds that this diameter is always bounded by a polynomial in the dimension and the number of facets. The preprint claims the opposite: that some simple polytopes have a diameter that grows faster than any polynomial.

The question matters because of the simplex method, one of the most widely used algorithms for linear programming. Simplex moves from corner to corner along the edges of the feasible polytope until it reaches an optimum. If some polytopes have superpolynomial diameter, then on those instances any edge-following strategy may need a superpolynomial number of steps, no matter how cleverly it picks its path. A proof would close off one hoped-for route to a provably fast simplex variant.

It would not change how solvers behave in practice. Simplex is known to run well on real-world problems, and other methods already solve linear programs in polynomial time. The open question now is whether the construction holds up under scrutiny from experts in polytope theory.
key_points: Preprint in OpenAI's GitHub math repository claims the polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false
Paper argues some simple polytopes have superpolynomial graph diameter
Result is unverified and not peer reviewed
A valid proof would limit worst-case performance of simplex-style edge walking
stories.why_it_matters: If the proof holds, no simplex pivot rule can be guaranteed polynomial on every linear program, settling a decades-old theory question. Practical LP solvers would keep working as they do today.

sources.title: HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT

stories.headline: Scott Aaronson says AI labs are now cracking math's open problems
stories.dek: The complexity theorist says earlier posts undersold the moment, citing claimed AI proofs on matrix multiplication, VP ≠ VNP and the Riemann Hypothesis.
stories.body:
Scott Aaronson says his earlier posts, podcasts and talks failed to convey the magnitude of what is happening in AI. His new Shtetl-Optimized post passed 1,200 points on Hacker News. He describes a run of claimed results posted to GitHub by OpenAI and Anthropic: proofs of VP ≠ VNP, an Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and an OpenAI claim that ω, the matrix multiplication exponent, is exactly 9/4.

Aaronson notes that the labs back their claims with Lean certificates. He treats proofs from OpenAI or Anthropic as correct barring evidence otherwise, and says he now feels a proof of P ≠ NP "is not far."

He also says multiple reliable sources tell him the labs hold cryptography "bombshells," but he declines to spread unverified details.
key_points: Aaronson cites an OpenAI claim that the matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4, with a matching lower bound.
He says OpenAI and Anthropic back their proofs with Lean certificates and simply upload papers to GitHub.
He reports hearing of unverified AI results affecting deployed cryptosystems but declines to give details.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic

stories.headline: Anthropic repo shrinks Lean proof claiming Riemann Hypothesis
stories.dek: A new GitHub version cuts the machine-checked proof to about 76,000 lines in compact form, but no mathematician has read it through.
stories.body:
A shorter version of Anthropic's Lean verification of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) result is now on GitHub, drawing 376 points and 192 comments on Hacker News. The repository describes itself as a Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of GRH for Dirichlet L-functions. It is built on Mathlib and uses only the standard axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

The work is based on Levent Alpöge's proof, produced with Claude. The author says the shorter version was made with colleagues at Anthropic and Claude. A readable edition runs about 300,000 lines, and a compact edition covers the same five theorems in about 76,000. A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory.

The repository states that the proof has passed machine checks only. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper accompanies it.
key_points: A readable edition runs about 300,000 lines, and a compact edition proves the same five theorems in about 76,000.
The proof builds on Levent Alpöge's work with Claude and uses only three standard Lean axioms.
It has passed machine checks only; no mathematician has read it through and no paper accompanies it.

sources.title: Google releases Cogentic papers on integer factorization, discrete logs and more

stories.headline: Google Research posts Cogentic-produced papers on GitHub
stories.dek: A new directory in the google-research repository collects papers credited to Cogentic and is drawing heavy discussion on Hacker News.
stories.body:
Google Research has published a GitHub directory of research papers it describes as "produced by Cogentic." The directory, inside the main google-research repository, lists two PDFs: "Nearly Tight O(log log log m) Prophet Inequalities for Subadditive Combinatorial Auctions" and "Polynomial Dimension Dependence for Fictitious Play Convergence."

The Hacker News submission linking to the directory is titled "Google releases Cogentic papers on integer factorization, discrete logs and more." It had drawn 475 points and 342 comments.

Unless individual subdirectories say otherwise, the contents are released under the Apache 2.0 license. The page carries Google's standard disclaimer that this is not an official Google product.
key_points: Google Research's GitHub directory holds papers it says were produced by Cogentic.
Listed papers cover prophet inequalities for combinatorial auctions and fictitious play convergence.
Contents are under the Apache 2.0 license unless noted; the Hacker News thread drew 475 points and 342 comments.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Google DeepMind AI engineers conjure mathematical proof of Signal's encryption protocol

stories.headline: DeepMind uses AI agents to formally verify Signal's crypto library
stories.dek: The AlphaProof Code effort checked an Arm binary of libsignal against its specification using millions of lines of Lean, Tom's Hardware reports.
stories.body:
A Google DeepMind team has produced a complete formal proof that a compiled build of libsignal, the encryption library inside the Signal app, matches its specification, Tom's Hardware reports. The researchers call the human-AI workflow AlphaProof Code and say it can be applied to other code needing end-to-end verification.

The proof targeted an AArch64 binary rather than source code. Gemini 4 Carbon agents wrote Lean definitions for Arm instructions, memory, system calls and Linux processes, then about 1.2 million lines of Lean checking the cryptography specs and 5.3 million lines verifying each binary instruction. Agents flagged 1 percent of the codebase for human review. "The majority of our effort went not into proofs but into specifications," the team writes.

Earlier efforts took far longer: seL4 reportedly took 20 years to prove, CompCert six. The proof covers libsignal itself, not malicious code added to an app.
key_points: DeepMind formally verified an AArch64 binary of libsignal against its specification using AlphaProof Code and Gemini 4 Carbon agents.
The work generated about 1.2 million lines of Lean for the crypto specs and 5.3 million for instruction-level verification, with 1 percent flagged for human review.
The proof shows libsignal works as specified but would not catch extra malicious code added to an app.

stories.headline: US jury convicts Huawei of trade theft, fraud and sanctions evasion
stories.dek: The Chinese company was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts but cleared of racketeering and obstruction; sentencing is set for September 2027.
stories.body:
A US jury on Tuesday convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets from T-Mobile and Cisco, bank fraud, money laundering conspiracy and violations of US sanctions on Iran. Jurors acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. Bloomberg, cited by Tom's Hardware, says the trial ran nearly three months.

Prosecutors said Huawei lied to banks about its Iran business, which it ran under the name Skycom. The Justice Department says it also stole from CNEX and Quintel, including part of a T-Mobile testing robot and Cisco router source code.

Defense attorney Brian Heberlig stressed the racketeering acquittal. China's Foreign Ministry condemned what it called US suppression of Chinese companies. Sentencing is set for September 2027. Ars Technica notes the verdict lands as Donald Trump prepares to raise tariffs on China.
key_points: Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts, including trade secret theft conspiracy, bank fraud and Iran sanctions violations.
The jury cleared Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027; the penalties sought have not been disclosed.

items.headline: Nvidia patch fixes driver bug that hammered SSDs
items.then: Tom's Hardware reported that GeForce drivers 621.14 and 621.24 reportedly rewrote a log file nonstop, writing up to 30GB an hour to SSDs.
items.now: PC Gamer reports a new Nvidia patch resolves the bug after an earlier hotfix failed to fix it.
items.next: The fix question is settled, according to PC Gamer.

items.headline: Huang, now back as Nvidia CEO, still faces December hearings
items.then: Tom's Hardware said former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang would face House committees on December 1 over concerns about an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, with Nvidia's lawyer following December 2.
items.now: Tom's Hardware now calls Huang the reinstated Nvidia CEO and says he appears before the Select Committee on China on December 1 and the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
items.next: What Huang will tell the committees is not yet known.
